#6271. Dust left by an exploded star holds clues to its final hours

Webb’s new view of Cassiopeia A reveals how dust from a supernova can preserve clues to what happened inside the star before it exploded.

Today’s Image of the Day from the James Webb Space Telescope shows a cloud of debris left behind by an exploded star.

Bright orange strands form a loose ring, with wisps of green along the edges and patches of pale blue scattered through the cloud.

The debris stretches about 10 light-years across.

This is Cassiopeia A, the expanding wreckage of a massive star.

The light from its explosion reached Earth more than three centuries ago.

Astronomers are now using dust in the wreckage to investigate a much shorter span of time, possibly just a few hours in the life of the star.

Cassiopeia A lies about 11,000 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia.

From Earth, the debris appears roughly circular. Within that outline are strands, knots, and clouds of material that took different paths to get there.

Some came from deep inside the star and were hurled into space when it exploded. Other material had already escaped while the star was alive.

One of the features astronomers examined is a structure nicknamed the Green Monster.

It contains dust rich in magnesium silicates and traces back to material shed before the explosion. Two other regions contain debris expelled in the blast.

One is dominated by silica dust and the other by carbon dust. A single image brings those different pieces of the star’s history into view.

As the blast expanded, it pushed into gas around the star. That encounter produced a second shock wave, called a reverse shock, that traveled back through the outward-moving debris.

As the shock encounters clumps of material, it heats them.

Warm dust gives off infrared light, which Webb’s Mid-Infrared Instrument can detect.

The orange, green, and blue in the image represent infrared light rendered in colors our eyes can see.

The shapes are what first draw the eye, but the chemistry comes from examining how the dust emits light at different wavelengths.

Different kinds of grains leave different signatures. With Webb, astronomers can examine individual clumps that would have blurred together in earlier observations.

Some of those clumps are roughly the size of our solar system.

Late in a massive star’s life, nuclear fusion can take place in several layers at once.

One layer may be hot enough to fuse oxygen while another, farther out, fuses carbon. Material circulates within each of these layers.

Under some conditions, that motion can carry material across the boundary between them until the layers begin to mix. Astronomers call this a shell merger.

A team led by Tea Temim of Columbia University found signs of that mixing in dust across much of Cassiopeia A.

The Webb observations build on X-ray measurements from NASA’s Chandra observatory and the Japan-led XRISM mission.

Together, the observations support the idea that the oxygen- and carbon-burning layers were already mixing when the star’s core collapsed.

That process may have begun mere hours before the explosion.

NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope helped the team decide where to look.

In a side-by-side comparison of Spitzer and Webb images, the older view catches the broad sweep of the glowing debris.

Webb resolves that same patch into narrow threads and individual knots. That difference matters when two clumps close together in the sky contain different kinds of dust.

By studying them separately, astronomers can trace where those differences occur across the remnant.

Some of the material scattered by supernovae can later become part of other stars and planets.

If two layers mixed before the blast, they could change the mixture of elements the explosion sent into the galaxy.

The dust still glowing in Cassiopeia A gives astronomers a way to connect what the star released with what was happening deep inside it just before it came apart.

#6270. An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Warming has intensified El Niño’s impacts on weather around the globe, making it harder to prepare

Large waves, driven eastward by the strengthening El Niño in the eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, battered the city of Oceanside California (shown) on October 9.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

In 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” says Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento.  And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

The El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

“We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

The neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves says. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

He reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

The havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier says. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a big boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”

#6269. New Congress will still be filled with losers

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

#6268. Weight-loss drugs have become more common, but not everyone has access

A study of more than half a million privately insured adults found that where patients received care was linked to whether they filled a prescription for weight-loss drugs.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are sold as Wegovy and Zepbound, and the two weight-loss drugs can seem to be everywhere.

Only 8.5% of eligible adults in the study filled a prescription for either drug within six months. Patients were more likely to fill one if they received care in areas where more residents had a college degree.

This gap grew as the drugs became more common.

Private insurance was held by every one of these patients. Coverage alone was therefore not enough to make access equal.

The study was led by Minh Trung Le, a research data analyst at Boston University School of Public Health.

He was based in the school’s Department of Global Health. Le worked with Andrew Stokes, an associate professor of global health at the school.

Insurance billing records were used for the analysis. Such records can show a pattern in who received a prescription. The cause of that pattern cannot be shown by them.

Stokes said insurers pay for these drugs far more readily when a patient has diabetes.

He called people with overweight or obesity “a population that has been left behind.”

The records were drawn from a national database of insurance claims. More than 175 million people are covered by that database.

From it, Le and Stokes selected adults between the ages of 18 and 64. They first met the study’s eligibility criteria between July 2021 and June 2025.

Clinical guidelines decide who qualifies for the drugs. The bar is a body mass index, or BMI, of at least 30. A BMI of at least 27 is also accepted alongside a weight-related condition.

High blood pressure and sleep apnea are two examples.

People with type 2 diabetes were excluded from the study. People on Medicare or Medicaid were left out as well, along with those without insurance. That left 512,389 patients.

The researchers checked whether patients filled a prescription for semaglutide or tirzepatide within six months of first meeting the study’s eligibility criteria.

Ozempic and Wegovy are the brand names of semaglutide. Tirzepatide goes by Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Versions labeled for diabetes are at times prescribed for obesity. These prescriptions were included in the count.

The clinics were compared through the ZIP code of each patient’s health care provider. Each ZIP code was looked up in the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey.

The survey reports how many residents hold a bachelor’s degree or higher. On that basis, patients were split into four equal groups.

Among patients diagnosed in the summer of 2021, 1.9% were prescribed one of the two drugs within six months. For patients diagnosed in the spring of 2025, that share had risen to 16.6%.

Even then, about five of every six eligible patients had no prescription after six months.

Semaglutide was approved for weight management by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in June 2021. Tirzepatide got the same approval in November 2023.

Both belong to a class called GLP-1 drugs. In clinical trials, drugs in this class have helped people lose weight. They have also protected the heart.

Both drugs were in short supply at times during the study. When semaglutide was scarce, tirzepatide prescriptions rose quickly. The reverse was seen when tirzepatide was scarce.

Le and Stokes took that as a sign that doctors swap one drug for the other. By the second half of 2024, tirzepatide had become the more prescribed of the two.

At first, prescription rates were about the same in all four neighborhood groups. The rates began to differ in late 2022.

By spring 2025, 21.7% of patients seen in areas with the highest share of college graduates filled a prescription. In the other three groups, the share ranged from 14.4% to 15.2%.

The results were then adjusted for age, sex, race, BMI and other illnesses. The number of doctor visits was taken into account as well.

Between 2021 and 2023, odds of a prescription were 15% lower in the least educated group. The most educated group served as the benchmark. For 2024 and 2025, that figure reached 35%.

Among men, the neighborhood gap was wider than among women. The overweight range showed the widest gap of any BMI category. Odds in the least educated group were 40% lower there.

For the most severe obesity category, the difference shrank to 10%.

Le and Stokes offered a possible reason. More illnesses tend to be on record for patients with severe obesity. An insurer’s approval rules may be easier for them to meet.

By the spring of 2025, 20.7% of women were prescribed one of the drugs. Among men, the figure was 11.9%. After the same adjustments, men had less than half the odds that women had.

Age was linked to prescriptions too. Adults ages 35 to 54 had about twice the odds of adults ages 18 to 24.

Black patients and Hispanic patients each had 11% lower odds than white patients. About a third of the records had no race or ethnicity listed, though. Those two estimates may be shakier as a result.

As BMI rose, so did prescriptions. Even so, most patients in the most severe obesity category went without one. Only about one in five of those diagnosed in the spring of 2025 got a prescription.

Earlier research suggests that early treatment can prevent or ease later complications, Le and Stokes wrote.

Among patients who first qualified in summer 2021, 1.9% filled a prescription for either drug within six months.

By spring 2025, that share had risen to 16.6%. Even then, about five in six eligible patients had no recorded fill within six months.

The forms for that approval are filled in by the staff of the clinic. Fewer of those forms may be handled by a clinic where staff are few.

Cost was named second. Different amounts are charged to patients by different employer health plans for the same drug.

In a 2026 study, 8,914 privately insured adults who had started semaglutide were followed by other researchers.

After accounting for other factors, researchers found that patients who paid more than $168 per 30-day supply were 9 percentage points more likely to fall short of the study’s refill target than those who paid $21 or less.

A review of approval rules and of patient costs was requested by Le. He also asked for help with approval forms for clinics that are short of staff.

Payment programs that reward clinics for quality targets were mentioned in the paper as well. If prescribing rates were made a target, a short-staffed clinic could be penalized for the shortage, not its care.

The ZIP code of the clinic was held by Le and Stokes for each of the 512,389 patients.

The income and the schooling of each patient were not held by them. The study therefore cannot assign the gap to the clinics or to the patients.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are sold to some people by direct-to-consumer sellers and no insurer is involved.

Sales of that kind are not recorded in claims and were not counted by the researchers. Which groups of patients buy the drugs in this way is not known.

A diagnosis had already been given by a doctor to every patient in the study.

Diagnosis codes are applied unevenly and milder obesity is often left unrecorded, Le and Stokes wrote. Some adults who were eligible may have been missed for that reason.

More than 60 data sources are combined in the database that was used. It was still not described by the authors as a match for all insured Americans.

The cause of the neighborhood gap has not been found. Insurance rules, prescribing habits and patients’ awareness of the drugs were listed by the authors for future studies.

Records of direct-to-consumer sales were also suggested by them, to show who is missing from the claims.

The full study was published in the journal Health Affairs Scholar.

#6267. The 8 Best Solar Generators Provide Reliable Backup Power in a Pinch

These tested and researched models from Jackery, EcoFlow, Anker, and other trusted brands are the ones we stand behind and recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel. Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.

Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.

Despite those distinctions compared to portable generators, there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two. Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

To pick the best solar generators, we tested some of these power stations for charging capacity, ease of use, weight, and different use cases. Our picks were reviewed by Popular Mechanics editor Brad Ford, who provided input for the larger-capacity units. Other models on this list were reviewed by test editor David Dritsas or freelance writer Maggie Slepian.

Our primary concerns were portability and convenience. Ease of use was also important—was the display easy to read? Did the screen readouts make sense? Bonus points if we could tell how much power is available at a glance. In the past few years, these criteria have become easier to meet. There are now plenty of compact, affordable units that have better charging capabilities than before.

Very few power stations of this size can handle as much solar input power as the Bluetti Apex 200. With two input types—low-voltage XT60 (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 (up to 2,000 watts)—it can accept up to 3,000 watts of solar power. If you had the panels and ideal weather, you could fully charge this station in less than 2 hours—even faster than plugging it into the wall. That’s impressive.

It also balances nicely between being a portable station and a home backup solution. It offers 3,200 watts of continuous power (it says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). We were able to power a refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and estimated the battery efficiency at 90 percent, which is very good. Meanwhile, the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity is expandable by adding up to six additional batteries. Using Bluetti’s largest battery, the B500K, you could build a massive 33-kilowatt-hour system.

While 3,600 watts isn’t enough to power a whole home, you could power a couple of circuits through a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt 30-amp output. But keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

As a portable station, the Apex 200 has a lot to offer. At 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. And there are several great DC power options, including a bank of USB outlets (two are high-power USB-C) and both 10- and 30-amp, 12-volt outputs. We also love that the AC ports can individually be turned on and off using the mobile app; this helps improve overall runtime.

Since very few stations can match its max solar input capacity, we concluded that the Apex 200 is definitely a top choice for anyone who wants a power station that can recharge using the sun’s rays, but also offers the versatility of being used on the road or at home.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review

This model replaces the original Jackery 1000, but many of the same observations made of the first model still apply. The new version has a slightly higher capacity of 1,070 watt-hours and uses a newer lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery, which is a newer battery technology that offers a longer lifespan (4,000 cycles versus 500 cycles for this model) and better performance in extreme temperatures.

Expert Maggie Slepian used the previous model on a media trip where she had to keep multiple camera batteries charged during a weeklong outing. She found that while the capacity was lower than you'll find with others on this list, it actually powers items for longer than some higher-capacity models. She also charged her photographer’s camera batteries while charging the power bank on solar power (it was a very sunny winter day), which proved effective and efficient.

The newer V2 model has seven ports, including three AC outlets, two USB-C ports (one 30-watt and one 100-watt), a 12-volt car port, and one standard 18-watt USB-A outlet. It charges a typical laptop eight times or powers a small refrigerator or an electric cooler for over 15 hours.

The Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 charges with a 200-watt solar panel or a 12-volt outlet in your vehicle while you’re on the move. It has fairly standard charging times, with 11.5 hours in a car outlet, 6.5 hours for solar panels, and just 5.5 hours to fully charge in a wall outlet. This won’t be your best bet for powering larger appliances, but it’s an ideal power station for smaller items and off-grid camping.

The EcoFlow Delta Pro is a large portable power station with an output that rivals some gas portable generators. When sold in a bundle with solar panels, like the package with two 220-watt portable panels we tested, it becomes a powerful solar generator. With an output of 3,600 watts, the Delta Pro can charge multiple appliances, and the output has the ability to bump up to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if more power is needed.

To get an idea of the run time, we used the Delta Pro to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator—which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes. When recharged from a standard outlet, it took only two hours and 36 minutes. But it also charges with the included adapter, at electric vehicle charging stations, with a DC car adapter, or with the solar panels that come with the unit. Through the 30-amp connection, you can also connect this to a transfer switch to directly power select circuits in your home.

Like any power station with a large battery capacity, it will take a long time, perhaps nearly two days, to recharge this station using the bundled 220-watt solar panels. The good news is the Delta Pro accepts up to 1,600 watts of solar input, so it can charge faster by connecting more panels.

The heavy-duty wheels and telescoping handle on Anker’s Solix F3000 are easy to use, allow you to stand upright when pulling, and are a dream for people who regularly find themselves moving their power station around, whether it’s at a campsite or to different parts of the house during a power outage.

Along with convenience, this generator is a powerhouse with the capacity to easily run your refrigerator or a greenhouse heater, or keep your RV bright and warm.

We were impressed with Anker’s app, which allows us to check the charging status or power being generated without continually going outside to check. The app also lets you turn the power to the AC and USB ports on and off remotely, keeping tabs on how much energy is being utilized.

The Solix F3000 has 11 ports, including two car ports, an RV-specific outlet, four AC ports, three USB-C charging ports, and two USB-A. In sunny conditions and moderate temperatures, it recharges with a 400-watt solar panel in just a few hours and supports up to 2,400 watts of solar input.

One of Jackery’s most recent solar generators is also its most rugged, able to withstand the elements better than most. It achieves this with an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system, which is part of a titanium alloy cooling structure that helps keep water out of the enclosure.

We got a chance to see these features up close and were impressed by them all, as well as a very sturdy enclosure that, thanks to the cooling system design, eliminates any side vents that could allow water to get inside. It feels strong; you could bang this station around without worrying too much about damaging it. The only downside is that this denser construction adds a bit of weight.

As a power station, it delivers 1,800 watts of output with a battery capacity of 1,536 watt-hours. That’s enough power for a weekend camping trip or for running low-powered small appliances and some lighting during an emergency. As a solar generator, it can handle up to 800 watts of input from a portable panel. We paired it with a Jackery 200-watt panel, and it worked well. Overall, if your off-road adventures often get a little dirty, but you need some extra power, the Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station is a good one to have at your side.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The latest version of the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping situations where dust, wind, and potentially wet conditions are always on the table. This 2,000-watt power station is weatherproof with an IPX4 rating and features outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs. Each section is well-lit by an LED light that’s individually turned on or off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a certain period).

There’s a healthy number of outputs on the Yeti 1500, including four 120-volt AC outlets, four (two are high-powered) USB-A ports, and four 12-volt connections. We simulated an emergency blackout and managed to run a cable modem with a WiFi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

To test its solar capabilities, we paired the Yeti 1500 with a Nomad 200-watt portable solar panel and connected it using the high-voltage DC input, which accepts up to 600 watts; however, it also features a low-voltage input that accepts up to 300 watts for smaller panel arrays. Because both inputs can be used simultaneously, you could theoretically pair with two arrays for up to 900 watts, which is a high amount of input for a station of this size.

Of course, no portable panel operates at 100 percent efficiency. Even on a sunny, cloudless day with no shade-causing obstructions, the input readings showed anywhere from 125 to 145 watts. After initiating a recharge with only 5 percent capacity left, it would take at least 10.5 hours in those conditions to recharge. That’s actually not bad. An average of about 70 percent efficiency for a portable panel is good.

This power station takes solar recharging seriously. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. We paired it with a 250-watt portable panel and, on a fully sunny day, got around 260 watts of input. That’s the typical efficiency of a portable panel (again, you’ll never get 100 percent). But pair it with some larger panels, and you’ll get even more.

It also boasts an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output, which is high for a station of this size. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper, allowing you to run small appliances and water pumps. It’s not enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

If there’s one downside we found, it’s that there’s no way to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 solar generator offers the right balance between a midsize power station that delivers a lot of power and run time, and a station that is compact and portable enough to be perfectly suited for an outdoor adventure.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review

The Anker Solix C2000 power station can deliver the full 2,400 watts of output to the bank of five AC outlets—something similar stations don’t offer. This allows you to power several things at once, like a refrigerator, toaster, router, and chargers, all at the same time.

During our tests, we were able to take full advantage of this, powering a refrigerator (by itself for up to 18 hours), along with some high-powered appliances, like a four-slot toaster and an electric kettle (though not the last two at the same time).

Another interesting ability of the C2000 is that you can fast charge it from AC power up to 1,800 watts, but that recharging rate remains consistent if you’re powering other devices at the same time (we confirmed this with a wattmeter). For example, we ran a 1,400-watt space heater while still recharging at the full 1,800-watt rate. Other power stations offer similar fast charging but will throttle the amount of power coming into the station while powering devices.

For solar recharging, we were a bit disappointed that this station can only accept 800 watts of input; other stations of this size accept more. But when solar was plugged in, it worked well. We connected it to a 200-watt Anker portable panel, and in full sun, we were getting around 125 to 145 watts of input, which is pretty good as these types of panels go. The C2000 is not IPX-rated for any type of weather resistance, however, so we would not recommend leaving this station sitting outside if the weather turns wet.

Full Anker Solix C2000 Power Station Review

Power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).

Meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.

That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.

For example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.

Keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter.

Just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.

Your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.

While weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.

That said, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase quickly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you plan to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.

I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.

This is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.

A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers.

A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.

Every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).

I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.

Solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.

Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

#6266. High school and college teams can win up to $20,000 each by designing technology for NASA’s Moon Base, and sign-ups close January 25

NASA's Moon Base Challenge invites U.S. high school and college teams to design technology for a lunar base.

NASA wants high school and college students to help design the base where astronauts will one day live on the Moon. The agency has opened what it calls a $1 million competition for student teams, and the deadline to sign up is January 25, 2027.

The Moon Base Challenge was announced on November 8 at a MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. It is open to student teams at U.S. high schools and post-secondary schools.

Teams do not need prior specialized engineering or technical experience. In the final round, they can explain an idea with a mock-up made of cardboard. Students have helped with real research before, as when students helped astronomers track a rare alien comet.

NASA is building a Moon Base where astronauts will live, work and explore in the lunar South Pole region. The agency says a permanent human presence on the Moon paves the way for future crewed missions to Mars.

The region may contain resources that could one day help support explorers. NASA plans to send a nuclear-powered rover called PROMISE to search for evidence of water ice and other resources there.

“We’re looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA’s future on the Moon,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute.”

“Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we’re looking for,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program.

Each team picks one of six categories: power generation and storage, habitat construction using lunar materials, life-support systems, surface mobility, communication networks, or astronaut safety.

Habitat ideas can go beyond engineering, since researchers have argued that Moon bases could be designed to ease anxiety and homesickness.

The designs have to work in a harsh place. According to the official rules, they must handle vacuum, radiation, micrometeorites, abrasive dust and temperature swings from 248 degrees Fahrenheit (120 degrees Celsius) to minus 274 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 170 degrees Celsius).

They also have to cope with day and night cycles that last two weeks each, and rely as little as possible on supplies from Earth.

Water is one of the hard parts: one analysis found that the Moon can generate enough power for a permanent city, but not enough water.

A team has two to five students and an adult coach, at least 18, who holds a formal role at the team’s school or organization, such as a teacher, faculty member or club advisor.

There are three divisions, judged separately. High school teams are for students in grades 9 to 12 who were between 13 and 18 years old when registration opened, including home-schooled students.

The other two divisions are for undergraduates at two-year schools, such as community and technical colleges, and at four-year colleges and universities.

Those students must be at least 16. A mixed team competes in the division of its most advanced or oldest member. Middle school and graduate students cannot take part.

Students must be U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents or foreign nationals who are full-time students at an eligible U.S. school and physically live in the United States for the whole challenge.

Every student has to create an account on NASA’s STEM Gateway, and only the student team lead submits the application. Coaches should not register there; they are linked to the team later on the organizer’s platform.

In the first phase, teams write a Concept Overview Paper of 5 to 7 pages. It must explain how the idea works and how it survives lunar conditions, and include at least one page of diagrams or other visuals. Papers are due February 22, 2027.

Up to 100 teams will be named finalists on March 11. They will then record a pitch video of up to 10 minutes, with a deck of up to 15 slides, due April 19.

Finalists can explain their design with hand-drawn diagrams, posterboard schematics or low-cost mock-ups made of cardboard, foam or household materials. CAD software and physical prototypes are allowed but optional. Winners will be announced on May 6, 2027.

NASA’s announcement calls it a $1 million challenge, and the challenge website says up to $1 million in monetary awards are available.

The official rules for the 2026-27 challenge, however, list a total maximum prize payout of $500,000, and neither source explains the difference.

Each of up to 100 finalist teams gets $1,400. In the final phase, up to 12 grand prize winners get $20,000 each, and up to 12 runners-up get $10,000 each.

The rules also say payments depend on federal funding and NASA’s final approval, and NASA does not have to award the full amount if too few entries meet its quality bar.

The money goes to a U.S. bank account designated by the team’s coach, who decides how it is shared. Teams keep the rights to what they invent, although NASA may negotiate a license to use it.

A virtual opening symposium introducing the categories is set for December 3. Registered teams can also join live question-and-answer webinars on January 14 and February 11, 2027. The organizers say all dates may change.

The challenge is run for NASA by the Institute of Competition Sciences. Full rules and registration steps are on the official challenge website.

The information was obtained from NASA’s announcement, its Moon Base page and the official rules.

Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl, but they are most known for their iconic howl.

The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place?

Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network.

Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other."

However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said.

When a wolf pack howls together, they are sometimes advertising their territory to deter other packs. "Data shows that packs howl more in the center of their territory; they howl more when there are pups around and also when they have a carcass from a hunt," Tamás Faragó, an ethologist and bioacoustician at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, Hungary, told Live Science. "So group howling can have a repellent effect on neighboring packs."

However, "most chorus howling is social — that is, they howl together to build what is technically called social cohesion," Kershenbaum said, "because it makes them feel good to be safe and surrounded by their pack mates. Faragó noted that this kind of group howling gets a pack in the same mood, "and is quite common before going out on a hunt."

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Howling can trigger more howling. "When an individual wolf hears a howl, it has a very strong tendency to reply back," Faragó said. However, "if a lone wolf is accidentally wandering into the territory of its neighbors, and they hear the pack there howling, they won't respond. That would make it obvious that it's an intruder there."

A wolf's howl can be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometers) away in open terrain, according to the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York. The combination of low- and high-frequency sounds that make up howls ensures that "even if some of the lower-frequency sounds are attenuated by vegetation, the higher-frequency components can remain intact and carry a lot of information about the individuals that made the howls," Faragó said.

Wolf pups make their first high-pitched attempts at howling between 2 to 4 weeks old.

Wolf howls differ among species and subspecies. A 2016 study of 13 species and subspecies of wolves, jackals, coyotes and dogs by Kershenbaum and his colleagues found that each has a kind of howling dialect that features different types of howls with varying regularity depending on the species or subspecies. For example, the howling repertoire of the timber wolf (Canis lycaon) is dominated by low, flat howls, while red wolves (Canis rufus) most frequently use high, looping howls.

The howling of dogs, which are descended from gray wolves (Canis lupus), can differ from wolf howling, but this depends very much on the breed. A 2023 study from Kershenbaum, Faragó and their colleagues found that more ancient dog breeds that are more closely related to wolves howl more often. In contrast, more modern dog breeds bark more often.

A question "that we all want to answer" is whether howling sounds might differ depending on their purpose, Kershenbaum said. "The problem is that most of the time when wolves howl, we don't know what they're doing at that time — they're either too far away, or it's nighttime."

Generally, "we believe that howls made in different emotional states probably sound different," Kershenbaum said. "For example, perhaps when a wolf is feeling threatened in a territorial conflict, the howl goes up and down in pitch in a different way than when the wolf is relaxed. But this is a field of active research."

A common belief is that wolves howl at the moon. "A myth, I'm afraid," Kershenbaum said. "There doesn't seem to be any correlation at all between them." He suggested that perhaps before electric lights, people were outdoors more often when there was a bright moon, "and that's when they heard the wolves."

#6263. Traces of insecticide in cord blood raise new questions about childhood development

A Japanese study linked insecticide exposure before a child's birth to lower scores on certain thinking tests at age nine.

Two compounds linked to widely used insecticides turned up in umbilical cord blood in a Japanese study.

At age 9, children with higher levels of one compound at birth scored lower on a test of processing speed, while those with higher levels of the other scored lower on a test of visual reasoning.

Earlier tests, given between 10 and 32 months, yielded no clear links after researchers accounted for the number of comparisons they made.

The researchers wrote that any association may hinge on the age of the child and the skill examined. Just 200 children took part. Proof that the insecticides caused the weaker scores cannot be drawn from this work.

Abir Nagata and Kenji Tsuchiya, a professor, headed the investigation. Both are based at the Research Center for Child Mental Development at Hamamatsu University School of Medicine.

They are also affiliated with a graduate school run jointly by The University of Osaka and four other Japanese universities.

The growth of a child’s brain and abilities is referred to by scientists as neurodevelopment. Children in earlier work on these insecticides were seldom followed beyond early childhood.

“Previous studies have largely focused on neurodevelopmental outcomes at a single time point,” Nagata said.

Nicotine served as the chemical model for neonicotinoids. Their target is a receptor on nerve cells that normally binds one of the body’s chemical messengers.

Insects carry these receptors and so do humans. Within a fetus, the authors wrote, the receptors assist nerve cells in maturing and connecting.

Harm to bees is what the insecticides are chiefly known for. Over a quarter of global insecticide sales are now attributed to them.

Food and drinking water have both been found to contain residues. Nationwide monitoring in Japan has picked up neonicotinoids in tap water throughout the year.

Animal experiments have been cited as grounds for concern. Altered brain structure followed exposure during brain development in those experiments. Impaired movement, learning and attention were documented as well.

Links with early development have been reported in several studies of children. Agreement between those studies has been poor, however.

All of the children are enrolled in the Hamamatsu Birth Cohort, an ongoing project on child development. The project recruited 1,258 babies. Their births took place in Hamamatsu, Japan, between December 2007 and March 2012.

Urine from pregnant women was the usual source of insecticide measurements in earlier research. What actually reached the baby in the womb is not shown directly by urine. Umbilical cord blood drawn at birth offers a direct measure.

Limited resources meant that cord blood from only 200 randomly selected children could be analyzed. Serum, the liquid fraction of blood, was screened by a laboratory for insecticides and their breakdown products.

Of the ten compounds measured, just two turned up often. Dinotefuran was detected in 104 of the 200 samples, or 52%.

A breakdown product of acetamiprid, a second insecticide, was the other. Its detection rate was 62.5%, or 125 samples.

The team split the children into low, middle and high groups for each of the two chemicals. Detection was seldom possible in the low group, which was used as the comparison.

Quantities were minute. A typical reading in the high dinotefuran group was 0.07 billionths of a gram per milliliter of serum.

The researchers scheduled five rounds of testing between 10 and 32 months of age. Depending on the visit, 185 to 195 children had enough data to be included in the analysis.

Toddlers with higher levels scored below the low group in a handful of comparisons. Large body movements at 10 and 14 months were weaker in the middle dinotefuran group.

The reverse was seen once. Hand and finger skills at 18 months were stronger in the middle group for the acetamiprid breakdown product.

The team ran 50 comparisons per chemical over the toddler period. Some results will appear meaningful purely by chance when that many comparisons are run.

Statistical significance was lost for every toddler result after the researchers corrected for this. Across ages and skills, no consistent pattern emerged.

A standard four-part intelligence test was completed by 178 of the 200 children at age 9. Differences on two of the four parts survived the same correction.

Processing speed was lower among children in the middle dinotefuran group. The measure captures how fast a child gets through simple tasks.

The shortfall against the low group came to roughly 7 points. An average score on this test is 100.

Perceptual reasoning was weaker in the high group for the acetamiprid breakdown product. Visual puzzles and pattern spotting are what this part of the test relies on. The gap on this part was almost as wide.

Overall IQ scores were lower in those same two groups as well.

Rising insecticide levels did not bring a steady decline in scores. Processing speed was also lower in the high dinotefuran group. That difference was smaller, though, and chance could account for it.

Tsuchiya said the contrast with the toddler findings may reflect links specific to certain skills and ages. On that reading, no single lasting pattern runs through childhood.

The children were only observed as they grew up, and nothing about their exposure was controlled. A link can therefore be identified by the study, whereas a cause cannot be proven.

A single blood sample taken at delivery supplied each child’s insecticide level. The timing of exposure during pregnancy cannot be learned from one sample. Neither can the degree to which exposure varied.

Adjustments were made for each child’s sex and age, premature birth and the education of both parents.

Diet went unmeasured, as did lead, other heavy metals and the parents’ own thinking skills. Part of the gap in scores might be explained by such factors.

Dinotefuran levels at birth were also higher in children who took the age 9 test than in the rest. The results could be skewed by that difference.

Too few samples contained the eight other compounds for them to be analyzed, alone or combined.

Only 178 children contributed to the age 9 results. The authors wrote that estimates from a sample of this size are imprecise. Weaker links may also have gone undetected.

Whether other groups of children show the same links is the next question. Why the links would surface at age 9 and not sooner also remains unexplained.

The authors called for larger studies. Exposure would need to be measured several times during pregnancy in such studies. Testing of the children would continue through middle childhood.

For now, a single group of children in one Japanese city is the source of the evidence.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

#6262. The libido drug women want is testosterone

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The FDA has yet to approve a testosterone product for female libido. That hasn’t stopped demand

One urologist says she has seen testosterone therapy for female libido "change people’s lives." But the data — and regulators — still need to catch up.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih says. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

The hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”
