Astrophysicists have dared to ask a cosmological question never asked before: Do black holes "wear pants"? New research shows how fast-spinning black holes may split apart.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black holes are known to collide and combine in monstrously violent merger events, but new research suggests these celestial stalwarts can also fragment into smaller bodies, like a cosmic pair of pants splitting down the middle.

In a paper published Oct. 22 in the journal Physical Review D, researchers used several mathematical modeling methods to propose a "pair-of-pants" topology for black holes. The hypothesis suggests that under extremely specific conditions, these dark behemoths could fragment into numerous less-massive black holes.

"Understanding precisely what is forbidden, what is merely unlikely, and what becomes possible once the assumptions are relaxed is the central goal of this work," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Black hole fragmentation could play into other cosmic mysteries. For example, it could help to explain black holes with masses that are too small to be formed through conventional astrophysical processes. These hypothesized black hole "morsels" would be so small that astronomers could see them evaporating before their eyes on observational timescales.

In the new paper, the researchers explored whether black holes' event horizons — the boundaries beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape — could split under various cosmological conditions. These situations included classical four-dimensional general relativity (Einstein's description of our large-scale universe as we currently understand it) as well as cosmologically esoteric frameworks such as higher-dimensional space-time and modified gravity scenarios.

But modeling black hole dynamics, especially the split of an event horizon, is messy work. So the researchers simplified it by comparing discrete slices of space-time, effectively condensing the fragmentation process into static snapshots from before and after the split.

In our classical cosmos, it seems mostly impossible for black holes to split, the researchers found, but they did identify a loophole that might allow it to happen.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The "pair-of-pants" topology for the fragmentation of a black hole.

The first impediment is entropy, the possible arrangements of an isolated system's energy, which cannot spontaneously decrease but only stay the same or increase. This has been theorized by Stephen Hawking and recently demonstrated through detections of ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, suggesting that a black hole's surface area cannot decrease.

For these reasons, splitting a static Schwarzschild black hole — the simplest type of black hole in our four-dimensional general relativity — would be strictly forbidden because it would violate the second law of thermodynamics.

The second impediment is kinematics, the motion of orbital dynamics, which precludes the possibility of a permanent split because the black hole fragments would recombine into a single body incredibly quickly.

But there is a loophole: A rapidly rotating black hole could literally spin itself apart.

"This is why, in four-dimensional general relativity, an isolated black hole in empty space could only split if it spins very close to the maximum rate the theory allows, what we call a near-extremal black hole," study co-author Manuel Del Piano, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southern Denmark, told Live Science via email. "Loosely speaking, the equator of the horizon is then dragged around at nearly the speed of light."

Through this theoretical process, the two resultant black hole fragments could be gravitationally slingshotted away from each other before they could recombine. So under conventional space-time conditions, it seems "black holes do not wear pants."

Then, the researchers mathematically modeled black hole fragmentation in versions of space-time with more than four dimensions.

In models of higher-dimension space-times, a black hole's rotational velocity is no longer limited because gravity weakens with increasing dimensionality. Therefore, any such ultrafast spinning black holes could theoretically fragment, the researchers explained in the paper.

A diagram from the new study illustrating the theoretical pants-splitting method.

In the "black string" model, a normally spherical black hole would become cylindrical or string-like, stretching across any extra dimensions. It could then pinch off to fragment into multiple smaller bodies, akin to "beads on a string."

Additionally, the researchers calculated that black hole fragmentation may be entropically favored in space-time models with modified gravity, which alter the gravitational interactions in extremely warped environments near the black hole.

"The fragments are tiny, though: in one of our benchmarks, a black hole of ten solar masses would favour fragments … a few times the mass of the Great Pyramid of Giza squeezed into a region smaller than a proton, and the heavier the parent, the smaller the fragments," Del Piano explained.

Fragmentation also may be more likely if there is a "bumpy horizon" around black holes, akin to a dense blanket or shroud of exotic matter that acts as a singular-but-gigantic quantum entity. The superfluid qualities of this matter could create strange vortices that eventually cause a black hole to fragment into multiple smaller bodies.

Scientists might see a black hole decrease in size, an actual fragmentation, or simply an indirect gravitational signature, depending on the dimensions and whether it intersects the viewer's "brane," or slice of dimensionality.

The researchers expect that smaller objects — like the hypothesized, miniature primordial back holes that may have formed shortly after the Big Bang — are more likely to split, compared with much more massive astrophysical black holes such as those at the centers of galaxies.

"Overall, we expect small black holes, such as primordial ones from the early universe, to be the most prone to splitting," Del Piano told Live Science.

Gamma-ray telescopes or gravitational wave observatories may one day offer evidence of a signal associated with the supposed split of a small black hole, but the specifics, including whether this actually occurs, are uncertain.

"One important caveat: our analysis shows when splitting is allowed by entropy and conservation laws, not that it actually happens," Del Piano noted. "As we put it in the paper, a shattered glass has more entropy than an intact one, yet glasses don't shatter on their own. Settling the question requires full dynamical simulations, which is the natural next step."

Cacciapaglia, G., Del Piano, M., Sannino, F., & Vellucci, V. (2026). When black holes admit pair-of-pants topologies. Physical Review. D/Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/cx69-t466

#6214. Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A tight bend in the subducting Pacific plate may help explain Challenger Deep

The ROV Jason/Medea (Jason shown here during a 2021 dive at the East Pacific Rise) can descend up to 6,500 meters below the ocean surface. In a new study, it helped researchers discover volcanic deposits in the Mariana Trench.

D. Fornari, WHOI-SSSG, MISO Facility, NDSF Jason Team, NSF

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern says. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”

R. J. Stern et al. ROVing in the deep: tectonic and magmatic complexities of the Challenger Deep forearc segment, Southern Mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science. 2026. doi: 10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

#6213. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

#6212. The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs Deliver a Bright Screen and Great Value

When it comes to color and contrast, OLED is king, but a great mini-LED TV can give you a great picture, too, often for an excellent price.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created. By shrinking down the LED backlighting that powered older TVs since flat screens first gained traction in the late 2000s, TV makers have found a way to deliver brighter TVs with richer, more accurate colors without relying on expensive new display technologies.

The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot new multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.

Just as importantly, they often offer great bang for the buck, especially when you're looking for a larger screen size—let’s say 75 inches or higher. As malleable as they are cost-effective, mini-LED is the secret sauce behind some of the best TVs on the market, even outdoing premium OLED screens in metrics like brightness and color expansion.

We’ve tested the top mini-LED TVs around, from entry-level options to groundbreaking flagships, to help you find the best options for your money.

I picked the top mini-LED TVs after sampling the best the market has to offer from brands like LG, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Hisense. I tested four of the TVs directly, while two of them were tested by Popular Mechanics staff and recommended based on that testing.

My evaluation was based on performance traits like brightness, color vibrancy and accuracy, image processing and upscaling, black levels, and overall contrast. For my testing process, I used objective measurements like brightness and color accuracy with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software, as well as subjective testing using a wide library of familiar content, from test demos to films and TV shows via 4K HDR Blu-rays and streaming. I also weighed usability features like smarts and gaming options, overall design, and size options for those interested in the ever-expanding big-screen TV market.

I’ve been reviewing TVs and audio technology for well over a decade at publications like Wired, Business Insider, Digital Trends, and others. I’ve reviewed virtually every kind of TV and display technology available, from budget screens to premium RGB LEDs. I’ve gone hands-on with the best new mini-LED TVs from brands like Samsung, LG, Sony, TCL, Hisense, Roku, and others, along with competing tech like OLED and QD-OLED, each of which has its advantages. Few things give me more pleasure than finding people the best tech for their money at every performance level and budget.

RGB LED, which uses tri-colored red, green, and blue light clusters for enhanced color expression, was the hot new display tech at the start of 2026. Virtually every major brand debuted some form of RGB Mini-LED, kick-starting a premium Mini-LED alternative to OLED.

When TCL introduced its own RGB TV for 2026, the RM9L, it seemed less excited about the RGB factor, and more interested in hyping up its exclusive new mini-LED tech, Super Quantum Dots (SQD). The QM8L makes it easy to see why.

SQD is an advanced version of regular quantum dots: tiny nanocrystals that emit pure, bright colors when exposed to light to enhance colors and brightness. Fancy tech aside, the results speak for themselves. The QM8L offers incredible brightness, far outshining its predecessor, the QM8K, alongside expansive colors that are as accurate as they are vibrant.

The new display offers other benefits, including fantastic black levels with very little light bleed, and reduced off-angle performance loss for most settings. Image processing has also improved, getting closer to the clarity and upscaling in top flagships from brands like LG and Samsung. The result is a premium picture that comes tantalizingly close to OLED displays in terms of contrast between the lightest and darkest images, and details that seem to pull you into the screen.

The TV’s Google TV interface is another plus, offering easy setup and extras like the ability to add albums from your Google Photos library as screen savers. Modern connectivity provides top-tier gaming features across inputs, and the sound isn’t bad either, thanks to built-in Bang & Olufsen speakers. Given that you can grab a 65-inch QM8L for as low as $1,000 or less on sale, it’s an easy pick for the best mini-LED TV available.

In many ways, entry-level TVs like the Hisense U6SF Pro are the best way to gauge how far TV tech has come in recent years. You just don’t expect a TV this cheap to look this good, from punchy brightness and naturalistic colors to minimal light bleed that lets you watch even challenging scenes in a dark room without being pulled out of the moment.

One sacrifice at this price is the TV’s black levels, which don’t look as rich as pricier mini-LED TVs, let alone self-lit OLED displays. Because of that, even though the TV’s brightness rises above anything you can stream, it can look less striking than step-up models. On the other hand, its matte-like screen does a great job of diminishing ambient light and even direct light reflections for a good picture day or night. That’s something I didn’t expect to see at this level.

You’ll get some handy features, including support for all major HDR formats and dual HDMI 2.1 ports with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) up to 144 Hz for PC gaming, another impressive get at this price. I find the TV’s Fire TV smart system a little clunky, but it includes some cool extras, like Ambient Mode that displays free artwork. TCL’s QM6K is a good alternative thanks to its friendlier Google TV smart system, but it can’t match the U6SF Pro’s performance, which is the best I’ve tested at its price point.

The step-down model of our top-rated QM8L, TCL’s QM7L offers many of the same goodies that make its pricier sibling such a rock star, but at a much lower list price. It all starts with the same SQD display tech, for excellent brightness and color vibrancy, and the kind of dimensional contrast that pushes mini-LED closer to OLED.

The QM7L isn’t quite as much of a powerhouse as the QM8L, but it’s still put-on-your-sunglasses bright, blasting well past anything you can stream, and properly lighting high-quality 4K HDR Blu-rays. Its potency aids in remarkable color expansion for a deep dive into advanced films like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Importantly, the TV also provides good color accuracy, along with deep black levels for excellent contrast. You’ll still see some minor light bleed if you look for it, and picture quality is reduced off-axis, but both are relatively minor concessions, especially for the price.

The TV offers a similarly loaded set of gaming features to last year’s QM7K, including options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) across two of its four HDMI inputs. Like the QM8L, its Google TV smart system is intuitive to set up and use. That’s all icing on a TV that comes about as close as I’ve seen to a premium display for the money.

Hisense’s mid-tier mini-LED TV doesn’t offer the latest display technologies like RGB LED or Super Quantum Dots, but it does offer seriously punchy performance, along with a design that feels much more premium than its price class suggests. That starts with Hisense’s latest anti-reflective matte screen that eliminates most ambient reflections, matched by slim bezels and a stylish pedestal stand with the kind of build quality usually reserved for flagship TVs.

Under the hood is a potent mini-LED display that employs regular quantum dots for rich colors and brightness that meets or beats anything in its class, including TCL’s QM7L. When paired with its rich black levels and reflection-repelling screen, you’ll have no trouble watching even darker shows in a bright room. Hisense’s image processing has also improved for enhanced detail and upscaling with low-quality content. I did notice that the TV’s local dimming may create some artifacts at its highest setting, but it’s a very minor issue. Like most backlit TVs, it also loses some picture quality when viewed from an angle.

Feature-wise, the U7SG is a gaming master, including VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 165 Hz across all four HDMI inputs, and handy extras like an intuitive game bar for adjusting settings on the fly. Add in its snappy Google TV interface, and you’re getting a whole lot of good stuff at a price that often falls well below $1,000 for a 65-inch model, and stays competitive up to a whopping 116 inches.

After skipping a year, Hisense’s flagship U9 series is back, now loaded with the latest RGB LED display tech for a striking makeover. The TV uses its tri-colored red, green, and blue mini-LED backlighting to great effect, providing rich black levels and sparkling colors that increasingly close the gap with OLED, alongside the kind of dazzling brightness that OLED can’t yet match.

The UR9’s screen gets an advanced version of Hisense’s matte-like anti-glare coating called “Obsidian,” which impressively repels ambient and even most direct light sources, making it a great option in sunlit rooms. Turn the lights off, and you’ll find great shadow detail and very little light bleed from bright objects on dark backgrounds.

Hisense outfits the TV with some premium extras, from a capable 4.1.2-channel speaker system to HDMI 2.1 support at up to 165 Hz across all three HDMI inputs. There’s also a DisplayPort for connecting a PC, though I would have liked to see a fourth HDMI 2.1 port as well. The TV has also gotten an update for the latest advanced HDR format, Dolby Vision 2, making it well-primed for the future. It’s all wrapped in a stylish design, for a posh taste of next-gen luxury at an accessible price point.

TCL was so confident in its entry-level QM6K that it was the first TV the brand released with its new mini-LED display tech in 2025, and the only major model that wasn’t replaced for 2026. That badge of honor is well earned, as the QM6K is one of the best-performing TVs I’ve tested in its price class, with naturalistic colors, rich black levels and contrast, and enough brightness to properly light up HDR scenes like a blazing sunset or a jet’s afterburners.

Maybe just as impressive are the issues the QM6K avoids. While most TVs in its class readily reveal issues like screen aberrations on solid backgrounds, light bleed from bright images, and awful off-angle performance, the QM6K mostly stays clear of those pitfalls so you can simply enjoy the picture without distraction. My only real performance complaint is the TV’s particularly bad sound, but given that nearly all TVs I test are much better off with a soundbar or speaker system, that’s not a big surprise.

When it comes to extras, the QM6K is well stocked with options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz for blur-free action and a gaming bar to adjust features on the fly. And while the TV isn’t nearly as bright as my top budget pick, the U6SF Pro, its Google TV smart system is more intuitive and responsive for a better overall user experience. With a 55-inch model now available for under $500, the QM6K is tough to pass up.

Most TVs on this list are available from 55 inches to large-scale models at 98 inches or larger, and at increasingly reasonable price points. A big reason for that is, unlike OLED, mini-LED TVs are scalable at a relatively low cost, so screens fit for large home theaters are much more attainable. That’s one of mini-LED’s biggest advantages over other display tech, not to mention the potential for next-gen brightness and color coverage at lower pricing. That said, ultra-large screens more readily expose performance issues, so it’s important to balance screen size with quality so you don’t regret your purchase later.

All of the TVs on this list offer 4K resolution with HDR (High Dynamic Range), and you wouldn’t want to buy a TV with lower resolution these days unless you’re looking for a very small screen (around 48 inches or lower) for a bedroom or office. The majority of new content is shot in 4K with HDR, the latter of which provides higher brightness and better contrast between the lightest and darkest images, along with the potential for more vibrant colors. Some TVs still offer 8K resolution, but because 8K content is scarce and difficult to recognize with the naked eye, it’s essentially dead (or at least dormant) in the current TV landscape.

As for refresh rates, any TV with 120-Hz or higher is preferred for fast-moving content like sports and, especially, gaming. All of the TVs on this list offer 120 Hz refresh rates or higher with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), designed to adjust to games dynamically to reduce lag and screen tearing/blur. Many TVs push to 144 Hz or better, but those refresh rates are only accessible with select gaming PCs. For consoles—PS5, Xbox Series S/X, and the Nintendo Switch 2—120 Hz is sufficient.

All of the displays on this list use mini-LED-backlighting, a smaller and more accurate version of traditional LED backlighting, paired with a liquid-crystal display (LCD). Because mini-LEDs are smaller, they can be used more prevalently to create better brightness and more dimming zones, which can enhance black levels for better contrast between the brightest and darkest images. Mini-LEDs can also be enhanced by features like quantum dots, nanoparticles that produce pure bright colors when exposed to light. Some advanced Mini-LED TVs also use RGB LED technology, which trades uniform blue or white mini-LEDs for multicolor red, green, and blue light clusters designed to produce purer, more expansive colors at the light source.

In contrast (no pun intended), OLED displays use organic material excited by electricity to light each of a TV’s millions of pixels independently. These self-lit (a.k.a. self-emissive) displays have distinct advantages, including the ability to create perfect black levels for enhanced contrast over backlit displays, along with much wider viewing angles. Like mini-LEDs, some OLED displays also use quantum dots: So-called “QD-OLED” TVs offer enhanced brightness and colors, among other new technologies to compete with ever-brighter and more advanced mini-LED TVs.

Both display types have their advantages. OLED is the best choice for those after a more balanced, nuanced, and uniform picture, especially if money isn’t a concern. However, because mini-LED is generally cheaper to produce, it may be a better choice for those on a budget who want the largest and brightest screen for their money. And in recent years, the best mini-LED TVs have increasingly advanced to better compete against OLED.

The most important connectivity option for gamers is HDMI 2.1, which offers higher bandwidth to get the most out of gaming devices. HDMI 2.1 allows for high refresh rates and features like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) from devices like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and gaming PCs. If you’re only connecting a Blu-ray player or streaming device, HDMI 2.0 will suffice. All of the TVs on this list also support HDMI eARC/ARC, which allows you to easily connect newer soundbars and other audio devices at high resolution for enhanced audio performance.

WiFi 6 or 7 may also be helpful for wireless streaming, especially if you’re watching a lot of high-resolution content, though you’ll need a router that supports those formats. Most TVs also include an Ethernet connection for a mainline connection to your modem. Other connection options to consider include Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, ATSC 3.0 for features like over-the-air HDR from an HD antenna, and an optical connection for older audio devices like a legacy amplifier or soundbar.

Each TV also supports multiple HDR formats, which is important for getting the best performance. HDR10 is the baseline format, which all modern TVs support. Most TVs also support dynamic HDR formats like Dolby Vision and HDR10+ (many support both). These advanced formats can provide a more precise vision of a director’s intent by adjusting the brightest and darkest images scene by scene, and even frame by frame. Dolby Vision is the most common dynamic HDR format for streaming.

If you’re interested in voice control, you’ll want to look for voice assistants like Roku Voice, Amazon Alexa or Alexa+, and Google Assistant or Gemini. If you’re connecting an audio device that supports spatial audio, like a Dolby Atmos soundbar or A/V receiver, you may also want to ensure your TV supports 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos and, for 4K Blu-rays, DTS:X.

Ryan Waniata is a professional writer, editor, video host, and product reviewer. Archaeologists discovered a stash of Celtic coins ahead of a construction project for an electrical substation in Hungary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades.

Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C.

The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said.

The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said.

During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground.

"This is a rarity in Europe," Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, said at a news conference, according to local news outlets. She added that the last similar find was made in Hungary in the late 1960s.

The hoard's silver coins are modeled on Greek tetradrachms — a very early type of large silver coin that was introduced in the late sixth century B.C.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The newfound Celtic tetradrachm copies are a type known as "Velem," which are named after Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement, or oppidum. Similar coins have been found at that site, which is located about 10 miles (15 kilometers) to the west.

Each coin has a stylized head on one side that probably depicts the Greek god Apollo, and portrays a helmeted rider and horse on the other side.

Artifacts from more than 7,000 years of occupation have been found at the site, including a glass bead (bottom, center) thought to be about 2,500 years old.

The excavations have revealed evidence of more than 7,000 years of occupation at the site, officials wrote in the statement. The artifacts include a nearly 7,000-year-old polished stone chisel used for woodworking and a glass bead with a peacock's eye pattern that seems to have been part of jewelry from the sixth or seventh century B.C.

A Roman-era villa was built at the same site in later centuries, without disturbing the hoard of buried silver, Kreiter said at the news conference.

The site in Hungary's western Szombathely region was excavated between 2023 and 2025 ahead of the construction of an electricity substation.

The villa has long since been demolished, but the excavations enabled the archaeological team to reconstruct its floor plan, including its underfloor heating system, she said. They also found a Roman-era brick with a dog's paw print.

The artifacts from the site will become part of a museum exhibition.

According to Museum Wales, the Celts were loosely related Iron Age peoples descended from Proto-Indo-European speakers. Emerging in Central Europe, Celtic groups occupied much of Central and Western Europe from about the 10th to the first century B.C. The Celtic Gauls were finally defeated by the Romans, led by Julius Caesar at Alesia, now in eastern France, in 52 B.C. The Britons were also Celtic, though most people of Celtic descent would not have recognized that name.

Several modern ethnic groups, including the native Irish and the Bretons of coastal France, trace their descent to the Celts. Regions with strong Celtic origins are sometimes called the "Celtic fringe" of Western Europe.

Writing in the Journal of Roman Studies, the British coin expert Christopher Howgego, an honorary curator and professor emeritus of Greek and Roman numismatics at the University of Oxford, stated that Celtic tribes in the Carpathian Basin, now in Hungary and Romania, started minting their own silver coins after Celtic mercenaries had seen them when serving with Hellenistic armies in Greece and Macedonia.

Howgego has written that the Greek-inspired Celtic coins included adaptations of classical Greek portraits, as well as distinctive Celtic designs. These copycat tetradrachms held very high value for their makers, so they were rarely used for everyday purchases. Instead, they were often hoarded as wealth or buried as ritual offerings.

Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6210. Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

It’s all about honing your instincts through practice and experience.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

Intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, says Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

Well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

“Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys says. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”

Intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

First, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

Second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

Sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

Since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

And the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

Your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her company, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

When working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea says. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

Overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

“It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys says. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more important at that point in time.”

#6209. Stellar nurseries next door

Clément Daniel from Pleine-Fougères, France

The Small Magellanic Cloud (NGC 292), a dwarf satellite galaxy of the Milky Way about 200,000 light-years away, appears to the naked eye like a fuzzy white patch, comprising billions of stars. But narrowband filters reveal it is also studded with glowing clouds of hydrogen, oxygen, and sulfur gas, many of them stellar nurseries.

#6208. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

#6207. ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Big Dig podcast host Ian Coss explores how Mitt Romney and Ted Kennedy worked together to reform American health care laws

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Big Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the issue near and dear to his heart: health care.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss says. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance plan in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

Overall, Mitt & Ted gave me new appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss says. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”

#6206. The Sky Today on Monday, November 23: Double star Kurhah in Cepheus

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 22: Flat-floored lunar crater Schickard

A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

If you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST on November 24, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon. A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars.

This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6205. This 9-Year-Old Owns Dozens of Vintage Toilets. He May Have Found His Calling in Plumbing—and Is Inspiring Others.

The U.S. is facing a trades crisis. Fostering some unique hobbies may be the fix we desperately need.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Like most kids his age, 9-year-old Damian Skaer loves YouTube. Unlike most kids his age, Damian also loves toilets, a passion he discovered on the social media platform.

Now, he’s a social media star himself, showing off his growing collection of vintage toilets to hundreds of thousands of followers across TikTok and Instagram: a pale yellow 1965 American Standard Cadet, a robin’s egg-blue 1963 Crane Oxford, and a 1972 Kohler Wellworth the color of an army tank. Standing on the 11-toilet, fully plumbed platform his dad built in the family’s Eastern Washington backyard, Damian points out their trapways, the fill valves, the siphon jets, the lid bolts, and, of course, the pièce de resistance—the flush.

Roger Skaer, Damian’s dad, says his son’s obsession began a few years ago. “He stumbled across these plumbers on YouTube who replace toilets, test them, fix them, and, man, he just loves watching videos of people working on toilets,” Roger says. “There’s been a lot of engineering behind toilet evolution over the last 100 years, and he’s fascinated by it.”

Damian’s collection began when he found a couple of old toilets in his grandparents’ barn. Since then, he has amassed about 40, according to Roger. Each week, new models arrive from brands looking to collaborate with the 9-year-old.

While the topic of young people and screens continues to cause serious consternation among adults, for some kids, they’re serving as an introduction to the skilled trades, occupations like carpentry, welding, and plumbing that have struggled to attract and retain new talent. According to a 2026 National Association of House Builders survey, only 6 percent of young adults 18 to 25 planned to pursue a career in construction trades.

But a crop of young social media influencers are bucking that trend. Guiseppe D’Anna has been working on cars at his dad’s collision repair shop since he was six; today Guiseppe’s Garage has a quarter-million followers on YouTube, and the automotive wunderkind is on “a mission to help shape the next generation of gearheads.” British woodworker Gabriel River Clark has been creating DIY content since he was 12, crafting anything from dinnerware to toys to home decor. On TikTok, 10-year-old Jackson Laux, a.k.a. Just a Jackson Thing, delights his roughly million followers with his deep knowledge of vintage tractors and mowers.

This kind of early exposure is vital to promoting trade occupations, says Paul Goodrum, PhD, a professor in Construction Engineering and Management at the University of Colorado Boulder. While lots of kids used to learn these skills in high school shop or career tech classes, over the past few decades, policy makers and administrators have phased vocational educational courses out of high school curriculums, emphasizing core academic subjects and college readiness instead. The best vocational programs, according to Goodrum, tend to exist in alternative schools for students with behavioral challenges.

“There is a bit of a disconnect between how we measure the quality of our schools and what the economy and the workforce needs in this country,” he says. “As an industry, we really need to be trying to more actively expose kids to these career paths not just in high school but middle school too.”

But it’s a vicious cycle, Goodrum says: fewer trades workers mean fewer teachers to teach vocational classes, “and how do you convince someone to give up a really high-paying job to go teach high school?”

The shortage of skilled workers is creating headaches for more than just hiring managers. A reduced workforce is causing construction project costs to soar and go over schedule. It’s also turning worksites into danger zones, as understaffed crews are working longer hours at a brutal pace. In 2024, construction workers accounted for about one in five workplace deaths in the country.

Most workers who end up in trade occupations do so later in life, often as a second career. The average age of an apprentice in a construction program is 28, for instance, while plumbing and electrical apprentices are often pushing 40.

“For so long we nurtured this culture saying you’ve got to go to college and get this degree or that degree, and if you end up working in construction it was because you somehow failed,” says Roger Skaer, a trained carpenter. “I think it’s a product of a long-lived, misguided representation of what success should look like.”

Recently, young people have started to question that college-or-bust narrative. Between 2020 and 2025, enrollment in two-year vocational or trade schools grew by almost 20 percent. And while the trades have their own difficulties—dangerous work conditions, wear and tear on the body—they offer something lots of other fields can’t right now: job security. According to the New Hampshire–based nonprofit Bring Back the Trades, more than 1.4 million trade jobs will be vacant in 2030.

Roger is confident that eventually Damian will fill one of those positions. “Right now, he’s saying plumber, I’m thinking maybe a toilet designer,” he says, explaining that Damian’s been angling for a 3D printer so that he can build his own commodes. “I truly feel he's going to be in some kind of trade or hands-on craftwork.”

And if toilets don’t pan out, Damian has a backup hobby: washer and dryer installation and repair.

November's full Beaver Moon rises on Tuesday, Nov. 24, giving us a preview of the spectacular Christmas Eve supermoon coming next month.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk on Tuesday (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018. These bright moons are just some of the many winter skywatching highlights headed our way in the coming months.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. Here's what's coming up:

November's Beaver Supermoon is just the beginning: It's the smallest of the three upcoming supermoons. December's full Cold Moon will be the closest, biggest and brightest full moon of 2026, bringing the moon closer to Earth than at any time since Jan. 2, 2018, according to late astrophysicist Fred Espenak.

#6203. Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”

#6202. Nov. 23, 1221: The birth of Alfonso the Wise

On Nov. 23, 1221, Alfonso X was born in Spain, the son of King Ferdinand III of Castile and Leon. By the time he succeeded his father in 1252, Alfonso was already known as a scholar – though he demonstrated his military might as well, putting down several revolts and annexing Murcia.

Known as Alfonso the Wise, the king pioneered efforts to translate Arabic and Andalusian works of astronomy into the vernacular Castilian. His multicultural court authored scholarly works and engineered scientific instruments, as well as collecting an extensive library of works on astrology and astronomy. Alfonso also commissioned the Alfosine Tables, astronomical tables based on Arabic sources and updated with new observations – facilitated by new astronomical instruments constructed at Alfonso’s orders. The work included stellar and planetary positions and became the standard for astronomy in Europe for the late medieval and early Renaissance periods.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.
