#6201. The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Researchers’ debate shapes how mental health experts advise men

Does “positive masculinity” exist or reinforce sexist gender norms? Researchers grappling with that question say the answer will help determine how doctors and therapists treat men.

Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” says Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health issues — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

The first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

That thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”

The higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”

Yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson says. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

He and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

But the study also showed that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their new masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work shows. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”

“I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott says. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he says. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”

Fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”

Perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher says. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales currently in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a new masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher says. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he says.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, says psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a new masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”

Such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher says. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis says. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

However the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”

If you or someone you care about may be at risk of suicide, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline offers free, 24/7 support, information and local resources from trained counselors. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

#6200. Americans Are Rethinking What Comes After Death. For Some, the Answer Is Becoming Soil.

The process of grinding up your bones in a “cremulator” may sound grisly, but it’s quickly gaining traction in the death market.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

In the United States, the way we think about death has rapidly changed. For instance, a 2026 National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA) report predicts that cremation will account for more than 64 percent of funerary arrangements this year. Likewise, an NFDA release from 2025 claims that more than 61 percent of consumers are interested in exploring “green funeral” options.

Some of those people are opting for human composting, or natural organic reduction. It doesn’t require high heat generation, it doesn’t take up space like a traditional burial, and it creates a natural source of plant nutrition. It’s a way to truly return to the earth.

In a human composting center, workers place a body into a contained ecosystem along with natural bedding like mulch and hay, and periodically tend to each habitat (similar to how you rotate your compost.) The process that Katrina Spade helped to design at her company—Recompose, based in Seattle—is modeled on one used to compost dead livestock; in testing, she hired a soil scientist to ensure that the heat of the composting process was enough to kill any pathogens. This happens in plant and animal composting, too.

At a similar company, Return Home, the process digests the soft tissues of the body into nutrients in the soil. Then the bones and any medical devices can be removed, and the latter are recycled. The company uses a cremulator, a traditional cremation tool, to grind bones into pieces. Like a coffee grinder or blender, the cremulator’s rotating blades turn larger pieces into smaller ones. The resulting finer particulate of bone is ideal for composting.

Today, people interested in burial have a lot of choices. That’s partly because strict laws and taboos around burying people outside of cemeteries or other designated places are changing. A majority of states allow burial on private property, some with caveats. Embalming is not required across the board. Even the required depth of burial varies a lot, and some states don’t have a depth requirement.

For some people, allowing unembalmed burial on private land isn’t enough. Many people will never own land in a rural enough place to comfortably bury a loved one. Cemeteries have been running out of space for a while, and experts say fewer people want the traditional American ceremonies linked with death, like viewings and services at funeral homes and churches. But that doesn’t mean people don’t want their death to bring closure, a sense of ritual, or a meaningful return to the earth.

Cities have long had unique challenges with human burial because of their population density. Neighborhoods might eventually surround cemeteries on the edge of town by the time they need to expand. Our parklike modern cemeteries date back to just Victorian times, when they were boosted as part of an overall public park movement in the United Kingdom. Even Brooklyn’s iconic Green-Wood Cemetery started as a public park. But while taxes fund parks, cemeteries are often privately owned. When they stop having open spaces to sell, they start losing income. It grows ethically murky very fast.

This is where human composting enters the scene. As a graduate student, Spade first introduced the idea in her architecture thesis in 2013, The Verge reports. She wondered if people in cities might plan to send their dead bodies to clean, organized spaces where caretakers could use nature’s own processes to speed up decomposition—or “recomposition,” as she calls it. This results in an amount of enriched soil, because the human body is full of nutrients like nitrogen, potassium, and phosphate that plants need.

It works a lot like any other composting system, or wild life cycle, such as a decomposing log or whale fall—when dead whales sink and become an instant food source for other creatures. Natural topsoil called humus hosts organisms whose place in the ecosystem is to digest animal and plant matter into soil. On the spectrum of humus decomposers, earthworms fall on the larger end, while microbes and tiny insects fall on the smaller end. Together, they form a food web, with each organism playing a part, like digesting a particular nutrient or a particular size of particle.

“Death market” figures show the overall rise in cremation rates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Cremation results in a small, tangible object that can be buried anytime, without the countdown to decay that even embalming can’t stop. For decades, the practice has been growing in popularity as a more environmental and space-saving way to prepare bodies after death.

But that’s not the end of the story. Traditional cremation requires temperatures of 1,400–1,600 Fahrenheit, the Cremation Association of North America explains. The type of ashes we imagine—where what is left is fine powder with some small shards of bone—is just not possible with a wood fire. While it is possible with coal or maybe an accelerant, at that point, the environmental catch-22 is pretty evident. Traditional cremation is better at saving space than it is at saving the planet—and saving space has had enormous value around the world for thousands of years.

The Financial Times estimates that each traditional cremation in the U.K. in 2018 cost about 150 kilograms of carbon dioxide; that’s more than a one-way flight from Boston to Paris. Traditional funerals cost many thousands of dollars on average, and burying embalmed human bodies in airtight containers has never been an environmentally friendly project to begin with. If you’re thinking about your future, there are more options than ever.

At Return Home, the “immediate need” package costs $5,950. The company also offers another option at the same price: pre-planning your funeral and financing it with a payment plan. At Recompose, the composting service is $7,000, with options for various remembrance services ranging from $500 up to $1,700. These are somewhat in line with current funeral costs, estimated at an average of $8,596, according to US Funerals Online, an industry resource company based in Delaware.

There’s also one wrinkle if you want your body to be composted after your death: Bodies cannot be embalmed before the process starts. The chemicals used in the funeral industry are “not compatible with” the natural decomposition process, Recompose explains, and many are carcinogenic or otherwise toxic. In other words, they aren’t safe to mix into soil that people will take home and use in their yards. If you die while traveling, you will typically be embalmed before you’re transported home.

There’s an interesting split over human composting, particularly evident in Christianity. The Verge’s 2022 article about Return Home leads with an anecdote about Sharon, a woman who had died from complications of multiple sclerosis. She was also a Mormon. True-blue Christians hew to an idea called stewardship, which is the way humankind must care for the earth and environment as cornerstones of God’s creation.

And today, that often includes climate change. According to a 2025 survey from Pew Research Center, highly-religious Americans are more likely to believe God gave humans the duty to protect Earth, even in comparison to those who are moderately religious. However, there is also a history of cremation being a contentious issue in Catholicism, though the strictness has relaxed in recent years. Taboos about burial did not stop Sharon, and perhaps won’t stop others who don’t take the resurrection of the body literally. To many people, even those who are Christians, the body is the vessel for what really makes human beings special.

Your reaction to the details above might be a good litmus test for how you feel about human composting. But if you think it sounds disgusting, and to even think about it is macabre—that’s valid! The vast majority of Americans are still choosing traditional burial or cremation. Today, human composting is legal in more than a dozen states, with legislation in the process in several more.

#6199. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full

Tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope. The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

The Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus, also in Taurus, at 2 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:55 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 4:24 P.M.Moonset: 7:10 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%)

Wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

Sunrise: 6:56 A.M.Sunset: 4:37 P.M.Moonrise: 5:24 P.M.Moonset: 8:26 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%)

Thursday, November 26Sunrise: 6:58 A.M.Sunset: 4:37 P.M.Moonrise: 6:35 P.M.Moonset: 9:33 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%)

Friday, November 27Sunrise: 6:59 A.M.Sunset: 4:36 P.M.Moonrise: 7:53 P.M.Moonset: 10:26 A.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6198. Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

“Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who currently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

Currently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., said Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper said.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC currently focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

Committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he said Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places important limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz said. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

However, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

“Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she said. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”

Luján also asked Thumann Severs to name issues where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she said her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Thumann Severs said that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

“Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any new Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science, 14, 1929806. https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

#6196. The amazing Crab Nebula

One of my personal favorite objects in the night sky is the Crab Nebula (M1). It’s No. 1 on Charles Messier’s list, although I don’t think he ordered his objects by how cool they are (a missed opportunity!). It’s not exactly impressive visually in most scopes — mostly a gray blob, or a spiky gray blob in larger apertures — but it’s one of those targets that if you know what you are looking at, it becomes immensely more interesting to observe.

The Crab Nebula burst onto the scene in 1054 C.E., when a massive star in the constellation Taurus collapsed in on itself in a supernova whose light was visible during the day, as documented by multiple civilizations around the world. Its leftover shell of gas and dust has been expanding ever since, and the bright glow is still visible thanks to what remains of the progenitor star: a rapidly spinning neutron star, known as a pulsar. The “crab” moniker stems from a drawing made by the William Parsons, Earl of Rosse, in the early 1840s with a 36-inch telescope, which depicts crab-leg-like appendages, although he later noted that observations through a 72-inch resulted in a view that looked rather different than his original drawing.

Pulsars are some of the most extreme objects in the universe. The Crab Pulsar, which is approximately 12–17 miles (20–28 kilometers) in diameter, spins at a breakneck 30 times per second — once every 33 milliseconds. At magnitude 16.6, it is a very difficult catch, but possible in large (20-plus-inch) scopes on nights with steady skies. It sits only a few arcseconds from a slightly brighter magnitude 15.8 star that guides the way. The pulsar produces a relativistic-speed stellar wind that generates synchrotron radiation, which occurs when charged particles move along curved paths, bent by strong magnetic fields. This is seen across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from radio to gamma rays, forming the main diffuse part of the nebula’s emission. This radiation has a total luminosity some 100,000 times greater than the Sun’s! The pulsar is slowing down gradually as a result of energy carried away by its stellar wind, increasing its period by 36 nanoseconds per day.

The nebula is still expanding, even nearly 1,000 years later, at a rate of 3.4 million mph (5.5 million km/h) — that’s 950 miles (1,527 km) per second, or 0.5% the speed of light! While not noticeable in a single observation, comparing images across several years shows the expansion on very human-accessible timescales.

The Crab’s intricate filaments are what make it so visually stunning in images. These structures are the remnants of the star’s atmosphere, consisting of gases like ionized helium, hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, iron, neon, and sulfur. It’s a moderately tricky astrophotography target to process: In wideband, it has a largely gray interior wrapped in red tendrils, so it is best imaged in narrowband, where it can display incredible, intricate detail that looks well and truly alien. A famous colorful 2005 Hubble image uses narrowband light from oxygen and sulfur and has oxygen-III set as red, sulfur-II as green, and oxygen-I as blue. When I’ve shot the Crab, I used hydrogen-alpha as blue, since it is a similar wavelength to oxygen-I (which are both red in reality) to create an image reminiscent of the Hubble one, much to my delight.

Whether you are a primarily visual astronomer or a high-tech shutterbug like me, the Crab Nebula is worth spending a little time with this month. Take a moment during your observing to realize how incredible this object is. Rising in the evening hours, it will be up all night for you to enjoy. How much detail can you tease out? Can you spot the pulsar?

Molly Wakeling is an avid astrophotographer active in STEM outreach. She has a Ph.D. in nuclear engineering.

#6195. Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The proof apparently settles a 167-year-old question related to prime numbers

The Riemann hypothesis reveals a secret order hidden in the prime numbers.

ROBERT BROOK/Science Photo Library/Getty Images

A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached. In a feat that will go down in mathematics history, a human working with AI appears to have solved the most famous puzzle in math, proving the Riemann hypothesis. The problem has foiled repeated and valiant attempts at solution for more than a century.

Now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20. The Riemann hypothesis, if true, reveals the secrets of prime numbers. In a statement on his website, Alpöge said he’d developed the proof alongside Anthropic’s AI tool Claude.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

By the next day, independent mathematicians had confirmed the result. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” read a joint statement from Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative.

A proof of the Riemann hypothesis is one of the most sought after achievements in mathematics. “As a mathematical landmark, it really doesn’t get bigger than this. I can’t think of a theorem proven not only in my lifetime, maybe in the history of mathematics that is as important as this,” says mathematician Ken Ono of Axiom Math and the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

“It’s an historic achievement,” says Bryna Kra, a mathematician at Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill.

Importantly, this was not the work of AI alone, Kra says. First of all, Claude had been trained on the work of thousands of human mathematicians, plus Alpöge was an experienced mathematician himself. He did not just ask for the proof then “push a button and wait,” Kra says.

Over six weeks, he worked back and forth with Claude. As an AI agent, Claude can use outside tools to perform tasks. The precise version of Claude that Alpöge used has not been disclosed, but the AI checked its work using Lean, software that converts mathematical arguments into code in order to confirm that a chain of logic holds up. It also had access to Mathlib, a library of known arguments already converted into Lean.

The result is 250,000 pages of dense, complex math. The world’s mathematicians are still working to translate the proof into a form people can understand. “What’s amazing about this proof is that it involves so many different areas of mathematics,” Ono says. “And I don’t know how a single human being could hold all of the ideas in their mind.”

The Riemann hypothesis, which dates to 1859, is closely linked with prime numbers. Prime numbers seem to be sprinkled randomly along the number line, but the Riemann hypothesis reveals a hidden order. At play is a mathematical enigma called the Riemann zeta function. The zeros of this function — the values that, when plugged into the function, produce a zero — are closely related to prime numbers. The Riemann hypothesis says that certain zeros — of which there are an infinite number — all sit on a particular line on a graph. If that is true, it would reveal how many primes exist below a given number.

Because so much of mathematics involves prime numbers, many other mathematical statements rest on the correctness of the hypothesis. The new proof will have wide implications. “It’s an earthquake throughout mathematics,” Ono says.

Alpöge claims to have solved not only the Riemann hypothesis itself, but a more general form of it, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends the idea to related functions. Though he guided the AI, Alpöge wrote that “what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater … Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.”

AI has been steadily felling major problems of mathematics, and this is the biggest one yet. But according to cognitive scientist Gary Marcus of New York University, AI’s genius at math will not carry over to more open-ended types of problems in biology, business or robotics. “In short, it’s not at all obvious that whatever Alpöge did has the generality many people are hoping for,” he wrote in a Substack post.

And some mathematicians have pushed back against the dominance of AI, disputing the utility of proofs created with the technology. The Association for Human Mathematics wrote in a November 20 statement on their website that no human being can claim to be responsible for the Riemann hypothesis proof, and that no mathematician can “confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct.”

Kra has been critical of achievements where AI agents worked largely on their own, independent of human intervention. The recent solution, by OpenAI, to a puzzle about the Navier-Stokes equations that describe fluids came about that way. But Alpöge’s approach was different, Kra says. “There is someone to stand behind [the work],” she says. She just hopes that people don’t see this as an end to math. “I think that this is a beginning, this is opening up more questions than it answers. … I think we have to use our imagination and find what’s the next frontier.”

#6194. Humans Will Go Backwards in Time Within 3 Years, a Scientist Says. But How Would We Know?

Medical advances could give us more healthy years. Proving they can keep adding time faster than we age is a much bigger challenge.

Getting older usually means having fewer years ahead of you. But futurist Ray Kurzweil thinks modern medicine might be on the cusp of changing that, possibly as soon as 2029.

The advances are arriving fast enough, he says, that every birthday could come with the gift of replacing the year you just lived. After that, he predicts, it’s possible that we’ll all start actually gaining time.

Kurzweil calls this “longevity escape velocity.” In a March 2024 interview, he put it even more dramatically, as going “backwards in time.” You’d still technically be getting older, at least by conventional standards. But your expected remaining years of life would go in the opposite direction, getting longer with each passing year as medical interventions improved.

Our earlier coverage took a closer look at that prediction and Kurzweil’s argument about how accelerating medical advances could get us there. S. Jay Olshansky, a professor emeritus of epidemiology and public health at the University of Illinois Chicago, has a less enthusiastic name for it.

“I refer to LEV as voodoo demography,” he tells Popular Mechanics.

Yet Olshansky thinks research into slowing aging could produce important benefits, too. His objection concerns the much bigger promise that those benefits will keep arriving fast enough to outrun aging itself.

Life expectancy describes a population, while lifespan is how long an individual actually lives. To determine life expectancy, researchers calculate how many people die at certain ages and come up with statistical predictions. Plenty of people will live longer, and plenty will die sooner.

That distinction matters when somebody promises to add years to your life. The Social Security Administration’s 2023 period life table, for instance, gives a 60-year-old man 21.79 remaining years and a 61-year-old man 21.04. Both calculations assume that 2023 death rates continue throughout the rest of their lives. They illustrate how expected remaining years generally shrink with age under fixed conditions.

Kurzweil’s prediction depends on medicine improving fast enough to beat those numbers, and to keep beating them every year. Imagine a 60-year-old who is expected to live about 22 more years. If treatments got better quickly enough, that person could turn 61 and find they now had 23 years ahead instead of fewer. That would be an impressive gain. But one year of progress wouldn’t be escape velocity. To stay ahead of aging, medicine would have to do the same thing the next year, and every year after that. Without that continuous progress, it’s just wishful thinking.

Olshansky wants to know what evidence would convince Kurzweil’s supporters that humanity had actually reached escape velocity. Beating one disease wouldn’t be enough. A treatment might save someone from one illness and give them more years, but another illness could still cut that life short.

Olshansky does see reason for hope in aging research. He says work underway “likely will yield reductions in the rate of biological aging.” That could mean people develop age-related illnesses later in life than they would otherwise, giving them more years in good health.

Olshansky would look at whether a treatment changed people’s chances of dying as they got older. Do illnesses show up later, and do people really survive longer? “It’s important that total mortality be the measurable endpoint,” he says. A treatment might prevent a heart attack, but that wouldn’t protect a patient from dying later from cancer. Researchers would have to count deaths from all causes to see whether a given treatment actually bought people more time.

Suppose a treatment delayed several illnesses and helped recipients live longer. That could change how people planned their later years, even if medicine never caught up with aging. People could have more good years after they stopped working, and some might choose to stay on the job longer. Before making those plans, people would need to know how much longer the treatment could keep them alive and well.

For now, gains in life expectancy have been getting harder to come by. In a 2024 study in Nature Aging, Olshansky and his colleagues analyzed the death rates between 1990 and 2019 in places where people live the longest, as well as in the United States. Life expectancy was still generally growing, but the pace of that growth had slowed.

Olshansky explains that much of the big rise in life expectancy in the past came from keeping children alive and preventing mothers from dying in childbirth. Saving a child’s life can add decades to a population’s average life expectancy. But in countries where most people already live into their 70s and 80s, those gains have mostly been made. The remaining deaths happen mainly among older people, and saving an 85-year-old from one illness adds far fewer years. That’s why it’s important to slow down aging. If researchers could slow the biological process behind many diseases of old age, life expectancy might start rising faster again. That possibility, Olshansky says, is what makes the research worth pursuing.

If only a few people received an anti-aging treatment, the country’s life expectancy wouldn’t change, Olshansky says. To find out whether the treatment works, researchers would have to follow the people who took it and compare how long they survive with similar people who didn’t.

And the only way to confirm a promise of 20 extra years is to watch people live them. “A specific prediction of a numerical gain in either life expectancy or lifespan associated with an intervention would require an observed gain of the predicted amount,” he says. Encouraging early results could justify more research, but they couldn’t show how much time a treatment added. Scientists could have good news in 2029 and still need decades to learn how many years people actually gained.

Even then, one success wouldn’t mean we’d reached escape velocity. Kurzweil’s prediction needs each advance to arrive in time to add more years, then another advance to do the same, and another after that. Kurzweil has said that people could still die even if medicine delivered the gains he predicts. Olshansky’s worry is that grand promises could overshadow the research he’s most hopeful about: work that could actually slow aging.

Slowing aging alone would give people plenty to look forward to, deadline or not: more years, and the health to enjoy them. Finding out how many years would take patience, because the people in those studies would still be busy living.

#6193. Pakistan’s first astronaut heads for China’s space station

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, Roscosmos is targeting 5:13 a.m. EST to launch the Progress MS-36 cargo ship to the International Space Station (ISS) on a Soyuz-2.1b from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, according to Next Spaceflight. NASA still lists the flight only as no earlier than fall 2026 and has not given a date.

At 5:45 a.m. EST, Arianespace will try again to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 Amazon Leo satellites. A problem with the rocket’s ground support systems halted Monday’s countdown. It is Amazon’s first launch since last week’s Vulcan failure.

Later that morning, at 10:55 a.m. EST, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has said what the rocket carries. The booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

That evening, at 7:18 p.m. EST, a Long March 2F is slated to launch Shenzhou-24, carrying three astronauts, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China to the Tiangong space station, per Next Spaceflight.

One seat makes history. A Pakistani astronaut will fly as a payload specialist, becoming the first foreign visitor to Tiangong and Pakistan’s first astronaut. Pakistan’s space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), has shortlisted two pilots, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud. One will fly and the other will serve as backup. The astronaut is expected to spend about a week on Tiangong and return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

On Thursday, Nov. 26, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) is targeting 4:35 a.m. EST for a Long March 2D launch from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Thursday, at 7:05 p.m. EST, Rocket Lab will launch Night Owls Never Sleep on an Electron from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula.The payload is a StriX satellite for the Japanese company Synspective. StriX satellites use synthetic aperture radar to image the ground through clouds and darkness.

On Friday, Nov. 27, CASC is targeting 8:00 a.m. EST for a Long March 6A launch from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

On Saturday, Nov. 28, CAS Space, a commercial launch company backed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, plans to launch a Kinetica 1 at 8:00 p.m. EST from a sea platform in the South China Sea, supported by the Haiyang Oriental Spaceport, per Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Saturday, at 10:50 p.m. EST, a Long March 6C is slated to lift off from Taiyuan, according to Next Spaceflight. Its payload is also undisclosed.

Finally, at 11:39 p.m. EST on Saturday, SpaceX returns to SLC-4E for USSF-380, another classified Space Force mission. The booster is again slated to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

Closing out the week on Sunday, Nov. 29, NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting 10:47 a.m. EST to launch the NG-25 Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Named the S.S. James A. Lovell after the late Apollo 13 commander, the spacecraft will haul several tons of science and supplies to the ISS.

Last week opened on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 5:51 p.m. EST, when a Long March 2D lifted off from Taiyuan carrying Shijian-24. China has not said what the satellite does; CGTN reported only that it reached its planned orbit.

On Friday, Nov. 20, at 6:59 a.m. EST, a Long March 8A launched from the commercial launch site at Wenchang with the 30th batch of satellites for Guowang, China’s state-backed broadband megaconstellation.

That night, at 11:20 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-317 mission from Vandenberg, two days later than planned. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You.

The week closed on Sunday, Nov. 22, at 7:23 a.m. EST, when a Falcon 9 lifted off from the same pad with the National Reconnaissance Office’s NROL-136, a day later than planned. The launch came 32 hours after USSF-317, SpaceX’s fastest turnaround between launches from the same pad. The booster flew back to Landing Zone 4.

South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD), the military research arm of its defense ministry, is still preparing the first full demonstration flight of its solid-fueled Mir rocket from an offshore platform near Jeju Island. After canceling a June 30 attempt over safety concerns, the ministry has said only that it aims to launch by the end of the year.

ExPace, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), also has a Kuaizhou 11 launch from Jiuquan on the books no earlier than November 2026. Its payload has not been announced.

This silver pepper shaker reveals the Romans' love of the spice and the lengths they would go to procure it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The pepper shaker was discovered as part of an ancient Roman hoard.

Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England

In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady.

The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum. The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending.

At the bottom of the pot, which rests on a four-legged base, there is a disc that can be set at three positions: wide open, closed and partly open. The pot would have been filled in the open position with cracked pepper and then used in the partly open position for sprinkling the spice over food.

The ancient Romans were huge fans of pepper, Neil MacGregor, former director of the British Museum, wrote in "A History of the World in 100 Objects" (Penguin Books, 2010). Pepper didn't grow in the Roman Empire, so merchants procured it from India. This made it an expensive spice, and filling up the pepper pot would have been costly.

A wealthy Romano-British family likely used the pepper pot as elaborate tableware, MacGregor wrote. It is unclear whom the Empress was meant to depict, but researchers don't think it features a member of the Roman imperial family. However, the fact that she holds a scroll could indicate that she was both wealthy and well educated.

The ancient family who lived near Hoxne seems to have left its wealth behind during the breakdown of Roman rule in Britain, since the pepper pot was found in a chest that contained dozens of pieces of silverware, 29 pieces of gold jewelry, and more than 15,000 coins.

"This was the mobile wealth of a rich Roman family — precisely the type of person who is in danger when the state fails," MacGregor wrote.

#6191. The Fed Just Warned That AI Could Trigger a Bank Run Faster Than Any Human Could Possibly Stop It

Since 1792, bank runs have moved at human speed. AI agents could change that in a matter of minutes.

The arrival of AI can be summed up in one word: instability. Since ChatGPT brought large language models (LLMs) into the mainstream in late 2022, instability in the job market has been a given. As the technology has required more and more resources, instability in utilities’ ability to supply power also became painfully clear. And as AI companies’ valuations skyrocketed in recent years, worries of an AI bubble have highlighted the instability of millions of retirement plans.

Now there’s another worry to add to the list: bank runs. In a speech in Milan last week, Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr warned that AI’s ability to react to a financial crisis at unprecedented speed could make future runs far more devastating.

“AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods,” Barr said in his speech. “Where customers once needed to execute transfers, AI agents could instantaneously detect yield differentials or stability signals and autonomously move funds at high speed, potentially accelerating runs that unfold in minutes, overwhelming traditional liquidity management and regulatory intervention timelines.”

Bank runs have been a fixture of U.S. financial crises since the Panic of 1792, when the newly independent country’s government was a whopping three years old. Banks don’t keep enough cash on hand to cover every deposit, but instead use that cash for loans and investments. But if the job or stock market takes a turn for the worse, customers might attempt to withdraw funds all at once, forcing banks to sell off investments at a loss, pushing them toward insolvency. After widespread bank failures during the Great Depression, the U.S. government created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to protect depositors. The Federal Reserve, meanwhile, serves as lender of last resort, providing emergency loans to banks experiencing runs.

These failsafes have typically operated at the speed of a human. But in a world where AI can pour gasoline on a financial panic by accelerating withdrawals upon detecting telltale instability in markets, bank runs could unfold in mere minutes.

And that isn’t the only concern AI presents to the banking world. Bank executives told Axios in late October that banks are struggling to distinguish between AI bots and human users, prompting them to restrict third-party AI access to their platforms. Major banks such as JPMorgan Chase, Citi, and Bank of America have already done so.

“We strongly believe there should be a human in the loop to authorize money moving out of your account,” Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC last month. “We’re working with the agentic agent providers to say, ‘Hey, you really don’t want consumers coming back and say money moved over from my account and I don’t know why and I don’t know where it went and the agent did it.’”

The swift efficiency of AI agents, tasked with squeezing every possible cent from a customer’s money, means they could also move money from non-interest-bearing deposits (such as a checking account) into high-yield accounts paying upwards of 5 percent. The problem is that banks rely on low-interest accounts to fund loans, so a sudden exodus would inject unwanted volatility into the financial system.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6190. The Age of the Computer Virus Is Over. Welcome to the Era of the AI Autoimmune Disease.

The cure for our cybersecurity crisis might actually be what’s causing this havoc in the first place.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There’s a quote often falsely attributed to Vladimir Lenin that “There are decades where nothing happens; and there are weeks where decades happen.” The cybersecurity world experienced one of those weeks earlier this month, and the ramifications have sent shockwaves through the halls of government and the average American home.

Was this an anomaly, or the first sign of an anarchic AI-fueled collapse?

People were already grumbling that the AI bubble was about to burst when the story of then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged indiscretions broke. Then, on November 12, Microsoft suffered a massive outage, hobbling an email service countless companies rely on. The next day, just as people’s inboxes were finally refilling, the FAA began grounding airplanes nationwide due to some unspecified computer error.

The demon in the machine evidently took the weekend off but came back with a vengeance on Monday. That’s when major disruptions hit banks like Chase, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America. America had been hit in its workplace, its skies, and even its pocketbook, but the final blow (for now) struck at a spot most Americans will never even see. On November 17, reports emerged that a significant outage had struck the NSA’s own internal, heavily classified network.

After that, the conversation shifted. People were no longer wondering whether the AI bubble would burst; they were asking whether AI would take us down with it.

In the aftermath, Congress decided there was no choice but to act. It was time to finally take a stand on AI that would prevent these kinds of outages in the future, even if nobody was terribly clear on just what had caused these disruptions, or what exactly AI had to do with them. There were bipartisan calls to assemble the “Superintelligence Task Force” to combat cyberattacks, and a series of amendments was proposed for the National Defense Authorization Act to limit China’s access to American chip-making tools, curbing its ability to produce malicious AI.

But what if we’re thinking about this all wrong? What if AI wasn’t attacking us at all? Maybe the AI was just doing its job, trying to strengthen our defenses, and its well-intentioned efforts had devastating consequences.

“Nobody ever asked: What if, in the name of progress, we were creating the ripest attack surface in human history?” Nicole Perlroth, a cybersecurity journalist and author of the book This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends: The Cyberweapons Arms Race, wrote in a thread on X. “We are entering a period of unprecedented technological instability.”

Perlroth argued that the official story being put forward by the affected institutions, that the outages were due to update issues rather than overt cyberattacks, isn’t a lie, and that’s precisely the problem.

What Perlroth posited in her thread, later supported by reporting in The Washington Sun, was that the AI these organizations had integrated into their systems had become efficient at finding critical vulnerabilities. Too efficient, actually. AI, it seems, had found “3X the number of vulnerabilities discovered in the same period last year.” On the surface, that might seem like a good thing. But it’s not enough to simply identify a weak spot—you also have to fix it before anybody else finds it.

“Mean time to exploit those vulnerabilities has collapsed to NEGATIVE SEVEN DAYS,” Perlroth wrote. “AI allows attackers to find/exploit vulns far faster than software makers have time to fix them.” Offensive AI tools like ARTEX can play a role in that exploitation, Perlroth acknowledged, but what’s likely playing a bigger role in these system outages isn’t an outside invader, but rather the system unintentionally damaging itself in a misguided attempt to patch the weak spots.

The rapid AI-powered discovery of these vulnerabilities “creates enormous pressure to compress patching windows and accelerate software updates,” Perlroth noted, “increasing the likelihood these fixes break things in unexpected, cascading ways.” In effect, the Silicon Valley adage of “move fast and break things” steamrolled the the principle of “first, do no harm,” long associated with the Hippocratic Oath.

Perhaps that ancient oath of physicians should make a comeback as we move into this new age of technology. After all, we’ve used medical terms for technological matters before; even the most “seasoned” senators and congresspeople on Capitol Hill have heard of a computer “virus.” That’s likely the framework lawmakers are using as they try to legislate the genie back into the bottle.

But a virus is a foreign agent, an outside entity that creeps into the body and wreaks havoc. What appears to be happening with the AI-associated outages we just experienced is more akin to a different medical concern: an autoimmune disease. In those instances, it is the body’s own immune system that, in a misguided effort to protect itself, mistakes healthy cells for harmful foreign agents and winds up damaging the body it’s intended to defend.

In the rush to repair these AI-identified vulnerabilities, The Washington Sun summarized, the organizations are “trying to push through a lot of patches all at once—more than the system was designed for,” and in doing so, are introducing entirely new flaws and bugs.

Knowing exactly what you’re dealing with can make all the difference when you’re trying to fix a problem, whether it’s in the human body or in a computer system. A misdiagnosis on either front can have catastrophic consequences.

Let’s hope our lawmakers and engineers have brushed up on their digital pathology.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.
